---
title: "Block-Eigen LD Operator"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
---

The block-eigen operator is a summary-statistics representation of linkage
disequilibrium (LD) constructed from selected PLINK BED reference genotypes.
It replaces one genome-wide marker cross-product operator with a collection of
within-block spectral operators.

The block structure, marker order, genotype scaling, allele frequencies, and
reference sample are therefore part of the statistical likelihood
specification, not merely storage metadata.

This page distinguishes two current representations:

1. the **retained low-rank scalar representation**, which is the canonical
   scalable block-eigen route for current single-trait fits; and
2. the **reconstructed-dense representation**, which retains the historical
   filtered block reconstruction and is also the representation currently used
   by the multi-trait block-eigen route.

Throughout the Methods documentation, mathematical cross-products are written
explicitly. Historical code names such as `wy`, `ww`, and `Q` are used only
when referring to implementation objects.

## Relationship to the Gaussian likelihood

For a single trait, the Gaussian summary-statistics likelihood depends on

$$
X^\top y,
\qquad
X^\top X,
\qquad
y^\top y.
$$

A block-eigen operator changes the representation of the genotype
cross-product information $X^\top X$.

Suppose the $M$ markers are divided into $B$ non-overlapping blocks. If
$\mathcal B_b$ denotes block $b$, with $m_b$ markers, then the block operator
contains within-block LD information but does not represent cross-block LD.

Conceptually, the resulting marker operator has block-diagonal form,

$$
\widetilde C_X
=
\operatorname{blockdiag}
\left(
\widetilde C_1,
\ldots,
\widetilde C_B
\right),
$$

where $\widetilde C_b$ is the filtered operator used for block $b$.

The tilde emphasizes that filtering or rank truncation can make
$\widetilde C_b$ differ from the complete within-block cross-product
information.

Consequently, block definition and spectral filtering can change posterior
marker effects, component allocations, PIPs, and other marker-level
quantities, even when the prior family is unchanged.

See [Core BLR Model Theory](model_theory.qmd) and
[Summary Statistics](summary_statistics.qmd) for the general distinction
between prior family and likelihood operator.

## Provenance and alignment

Public block-eigen fitters require enough information to establish the
relationship among:

- the selected PLINK BED reference genotypes;
- selected individuals;
- selected markers and their order;
- block boundaries;
- allele frequencies;
- genotype standardization;
- summary-statistic marker order; and
- the block-eigen operator constructed from those inputs.

The operator is therefore not an interchangeable LD file independent of the
summary statistics.

Current multi-trait block-eigen use is more restrictive: the summary
statistics are required to be derived from the same selected BED genotypes by
construction. Arbitrary projection of an external GWAS onto an independently
constructed block-eigen reference is not part of the current public contract.

## Block construction

Markers and samples are resolved once from `Glist`, `rows`, and the selected BED
columns.

BED genotypes are decoded, missing values are handled according to the aligned
allele-frequency and standardization contract, and the selected marker columns
are placed on the standardized-genotype scale.

At the public R boundary, `block_start` uses one-based indexing.

The blocks must be:

- positive;
- contiguous;
- non-overlapping; and
- exhaustive over the selected marker order.

A marker belongs to exactly one block.

Cross-block LD is therefore set to zero by the operator definition.

## Within-block eigendecomposition

For block $b$, let $C_b$ denote the standardized within-block
cross-product/correlation representation constructed by the implementation.

After symmetrization, the block is eigendecomposed as

$$
C_b
=
U_b\Lambda_bU_b^\top,
$$

where $\Lambda_b$ contains the block eigenvalues and $U_b$ the corresponding
eigenvectors.

The subsequent representation depends on the chosen block-eigen mode.

## Retained low-rank scalar representation

For current scalar fits, `representation = "low_rank"` is the canonical
block-eigen representation.

The implementation retains only positive eigenvalues above

$$
10^{-10}.
$$

Among those positive eigenvalues, it chooses the smallest leading rank $k_b$
whose cumulative positive-eigenvalue mass is **strictly greater than**

$$
\texttt{eigen_prop}.
$$

The public default is

$$
\texttt{eigen_prop}=0.995.
$$

The strict inequality is important. If the cumulative retained mass lands
exactly on the requested boundary, the next eigenvector is retained.

Zero or negative eigenvalues are omitted. A block whose retained rank is zero
fails rather than silently producing an empty operator.

### What is stored

The scalar low-rank implementation stores:

- a retained eigen-by-marker factor `Q` for each block;
- a transformed marker score;
- the runtime marker diagonal; and
- one reduced residual state per chain.

If block $b$ contains $m_b$ markers and retains rank $k_b$, the factor has
dimension

$$
k_b\times m_b.
$$

The immutable retained factor and transformed score are shared across logical
chains. Each chain owns its own reduced residual and sampler state.

The retained factor is constructed in double precision and stored in
single-precision column-major form; transformed scores and chain residuals are
kept in double precision.

### Computational scaling

A marker update costs approximately the retained rank of its block rather than
the full block size.

The retained-factor storage scales as

$$
O\left(
\sum_{b=1}^{B}m_bk_b
\right).
$$

This gives a substantial memory and computational advantage only when

$$
k_b\ll m_b
$$

for a meaningful fraction of the blocks.

If nearly all modes are retained, the low-rank representation provides little
compression.

## Relationship to the GCTB/SBayesRC eigenspace likelihood

The retained scalar operator follows the GCTB/SBayesRC eigenspace-likelihood
strategy, represented in `sblr` cross-product units.

The following parts have an explicit scale crosswalk to the pinned GCTB
reference implementation:

- retained-rank construction;
- transformed score representation; and
- marker conditional calculations.

The residual-variance update is not identical.

Current `sblr` scalar block-eigen fitting uses one global projected residual
sum-of-squares contract.

The referenced GCTB procedure instead uses block-specific residual-variance
quantities involving:

- block sample sizes;
- retained-rank degrees of freedom; and
- block-specific residual variances.

Therefore, agreement in retained eigenspace construction does not imply that
the complete residual-variance procedure is identical.

## Reconstructed-dense representation

The historical scalar reference route remains available as

```r
representation = "dense_reconstructed"
```

and the current multi-trait block-eigen route also uses reconstructed filtered
within-block operators rather than the scalar retained-factor runtime.

The reconstructed representation stores a filtered dense operator for each
block in packed symmetric form.

Three filtering policies are retained.

### Hard truncation

With `hard_truncate`, eigenvalues below the nonnegative `eigen_tau` threshold
are removed.

The summary score $X^\top y$, represented in the current ST interface by
`wy`, is projected consistently into the retained eigenspace.

Thus both the block operator and the marker score are restricted to the retained
spectral subspace.

### Fixed ridge

With `ridge_fixed`, a fixed nonnegative `eigen_eta` ridge/shrinkage rule is
applied.

Unlike hard truncation, the summary score remains on its original aligned
scale. In other words, the filtering rule modifies the block operator without
hard-projecting the score into a reduced eigenspace.

### Ledoit-Wolf-style shrinkage

With `ridge_lw`, a block-specific Ledoit-Wolf-style shrinkage estimate is used
together with the implementation's positive numerical floor and block
diagnostics.

The summary score is not hard projected.

These filtering policies define different likelihood operators and should be
reported as part of the model specification.

## Dense reconstructed runtime storage

For reconstructed block $b$, the symmetric filtered operator is stored using
the packed upper triangle in single precision.

The implementation additionally retains:

- marker-to-block mappings;
- within-block marker indices; and
- a double-precision runtime diagonal.

Immutable block storage is prepared once and borrowed by the logical chains.
Worker tasks own sampler state but do not rebuild or copy the operator.

The packed storage scales as

$$
O\left(
\sum_{b=1}^{B}
\frac{m_b(m_b+1)}{2}
\right).
$$

A marker update visits the within-block off-diagonal entries associated with
that marker, so the update cost is proportional to block size.

This is a dense within-block representation. It is not low-rank storage.

Narrower blocks reduce memory and update cost, but they also remove more
cross-block LD by construction.

## Three different diagonal quantities

Three marker diagonals appear in the block-eigen workflow and must not be
conflated.

### Input summary-statistic diagonal

The input `ww` records the marker diagonal information supplied with the
summary statistics. Mathematically, it corresponds to

$$
\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X)
$$

under the summary-statistic genotype representation.

### Unfiltered reference diagonal

Before spectral filtering, the BED-derived within-block operator has its own
reference diagonal.

This records the marker information implied by the selected block-eigen
reference construction before filtering.

### Filtered runtime diagonal

After eigenspace truncation or shrinkage, the operator used by the sampler has
a filtered runtime diagonal,

$$
\operatorname{diag}(\widetilde C_X).
$$

This is the diagonal that belongs to the actual likelihood operator used during
marker updates.

The block-eigen summary route validates input `ww` as provenance. It does not
silently replace the filtered runtime diagonal with the input summary-statistic
diagonal.

For the reconstructed representation, the runtime diagonal exactly matches the
diagonal of the packed filtered block operator and is required to remain
positive.

This distinction matters because spectral filtering changes the operator.
Using an unfiltered diagonal together with a filtered off-diagonal operator
would define a different marker conditional.

## Effect on marker updates

Under a complete cross-product representation, the marker-scale residual score
is

$$
r
=
X^\top y-X^\top Xb.
$$

Under a block-eigen operator, the likelihood instead uses its filtered
block-based representation.

Conceptually, the corresponding score becomes

$$
r_{\mathrm{block}}
=
X^\top y-\widetilde C_Xb
$$

for a reconstructed block operator, or the mathematically equivalent reduced
state in the retained-factor representation.

Thus, spectral truncation or block partitioning affects the way effect changes
propagate through LD.

This is why block-eigen filtering is not merely a compression choice: it changes
the likelihood information retained by the sampler.

## Block boundaries

Block boundaries create another approximation independent of spectral
filtering.

Even if every positive eigenmode is retained within each block, the operator
still omits correlations between markers in different blocks.

Therefore two distinct approximations can be present:

1. **block approximation:** cross-block LD is set to zero;
2. **spectral approximation:** within-block modes are filtered, truncated, or
   shrunk.

These choices should be distinguished when comparing block-eigen results with
CSR or other LD representations.

## Public support

Current public block-eigen fitting includes:

### Single trait

`stblr_block_eigen()` supports ordinary:

- `sbayesc`;
- `sbayesr`; and
- `sbayesrc`.

The scalar block-eigen route also supports the qualified BayesC-LV and
BayesR-LV annotation log-variance models.

The retained-factor representation is the canonical scalable scalar route. The
historical reconstructed-dense scalar representation remains available for
reference and explicit use.

### Multi trait

`mtblr_block_eigen()` supports:

- `sbayesc`;
- `sbayesr`; and
- `sbayesrc`.

The current MT block-eigen runtime is reconstructed dense. A retained-factor MT
runtime is not currently implemented.

MT-LV is also not currently implemented.

These capability distinctions are model/operator facts; they should not be
inferred merely from the presence of similarly named arguments on another
route.

## Example calls

The canonical scalar route is:

```r
fit <- stblr_block_eigen(
  stats = stats,
  Glist = Glist,
  block_start = block_start,
  method = "sbayesr"
)
```

The historical reconstructed-dense scalar route can be requested explicitly:

```r
fit_dense_reference <- stblr_block_eigen(
  stats = stats,
  Glist = Glist,
  block_start = block_start,
  method = "sbayesr",
  representation = "dense_reconstructed"
)
```

For current annotation-dependent BayesRC/SBayesRC routes, use the arguments
documented by the corresponding public fitter.

The ST and MT interfaces currently differ in some historical argument naming
for annotation inputs. Those are code/API conventions rather than different
statistical annotation objects.

## MAF-S and allele-frequency provenance

Fixed `maf_effect_s` requires aligned allele frequencies and explicit
provenance.

MAF-S modifies the active-effect prior variance, whereas the block-eigen
operator modifies the likelihood representation.

The two therefore affect different parts of the posterior model.

See [Annotation-Informed Priors](annotation_priors.qmd) for the mathematical
MAF-S variance architecture.

## Reduction and operator comparison

Exact or nearly unfiltered block construction is useful for validating the
operator against another likelihood representation.

Permanent reductions compare block-eigen and CSR behavior when both are
constructed to represent the same LD information.

Such comparisons test operator consistency. They should not be interpreted as
proof that aggressively filtered block-eigen, thresholded CSR, and complete
individual-level likelihoods are identical models.

Agreement depends on:

- the same marker set and order;
- the same allele orientation;
- compatible genotype scaling;
- compatible sample/reference construction;
- equivalent retained LD information; and
- matching priors and update settings.

## Consequences for fine-mapping

Marker-level posterior quantities are particularly sensitive to local LD.

Spectral filtering, block boundaries, and reconstruction choices can therefore
affect:

- which correlated marker receives posterior mass;
- PIP ranking;
- posterior component allocation;
- posterior mean effects; and
- marginal-PIP credible-set post-processing.

A block-eigen fit and a sparse-CSR fit can agree well at the level of genomic
prediction while differing more noticeably in local marker allocation.

This does not necessarily imply a sampler error; it can reflect genuinely
different LD information in the likelihood operators.

See [Fine-Mapping and Credible Sets](fine_mapping.qmd) for the interpretation
of marginal PIPs and LD-aware post-processing.

## Practical limitations

Important limitations of the current block-eigen operator include:

- cross-block LD is not represented;
- spectral filtering changes the likelihood operator;
- the retained representation is efficient only when retained rank is
  materially below block size;
- reconstructed dense blocks can become expensive for large blocks;
- current arbitrary external-GWAS/reference-LD projection is not supported by
  the public block-eigen contract;
- current MT block-eigen fitting remains reconstructed dense rather than
  retained-factor;
- reference sample, marker order, allele orientation, missing-value handling,
  allele frequencies, block boundaries, and filter settings are required
  provenance.

Depending on block size, retained rank, and LD sparsity, sparse CSR or packed
dense block representations may be more efficient than retained factors.

## Reporting recommendations

A block-eigen analysis should report at least:

- the BED/reference sample used to construct the operator;
- selected sample and marker definitions;
- genotype scaling and allele-frequency source;
- block boundaries;
- representation (`low_rank` or `dense_reconstructed`);
- retained-rank threshold `eigen_prop` for low rank;
- filter policy and parameters for reconstructed dense blocks;
- retained ranks or relevant block diagnostics;
- whether the analysis is ST or MT;
- whether MAF-S or annotation-informed priors were used; and
- the provenance relationship between the summary statistics and the
  block-eigen reference.

These quantities define the statistical operator sufficiently to interpret
differences among fits.

This page therefore owns the statistical interpretation of the block-eigen
likelihood operator: block boundaries remove cross-block LD, spectral filtering
changes the within-block operator, retained factors provide a scalable scalar
runtime when rank is genuinely reduced, and the reconstructed-dense route
remains the current reference representation for historical scalar use and
multi-trait fitting.
